analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes from forcing residents to sign away their right to sue before disputes arise.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal arbitration law to make pre-dispute arbitration agreements between long-term care facilities and their residents invalid and unenforceable. Nursing homes often ask residents—or family members signing on their behalf—to agree to arbitration at admission, before any dispute exists. The bill would leave residents free to file arbitration voluntarily after a dispute arises, but unable to be forced into it by a contract signed at the door. It applies to skilled nursing facilities, nursing facilities, and assisted-living-type facilities providing help with daily activities.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home and long-term care residents and their families. Arbitration clauses signed at admission are frequently contested on the grounds that residents or their families sign them under time pressure and without understanding, and that arbitration keeps claims of neglect, abuse, or wrongful death out of public court, where juries can award larger damages and records are public. The bill would let residents take those claims to court if they chose to, and it would let a judge—not an arbitrator—decide whether the arbitration agreement is valid in the first place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: A pre-dispute arbitration agreement between a long-term care facility and a resident, or a person acting on the resident's behalf such as someone with financial responsibility, would not be valid or specifically enforceable [S2, S3].
The ban covers agreements signed during or after the admission process, closing the common practice of having residents or family members sign an arbitration clause at move-in [S3].

The bill defines covered facilities broadly, including skilled nursing facilities, nursing facilities under the Social Security Act, and proprietary, public, or nonprofit facilities providing help with bathing, dressing, eating, and medication—i.e., assisted living as well as nursing homes [S3].
It would be a court, not an arbitrator, that decides whether the federal ban applies to a given agreement, keeping the question out of the private arbitration system itself [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Long-term care facilities, including for-profit nursing home chains, would lose a tool they use to manage legal exposure: arbitration clauses tend to cap damages, keep proceedings confidential, and remove the risk of a jury verdict in abuse or neglect cases. Facilities could face more lawsuits in open court, and higher liability costs could eventually feed back into the prices they charge residents and bill to public programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home and long-term care operators

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is cost: facilities and their insurers argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than litigation and that eliminating it for an entire industry raises liability costs that get passed on through higher prices for care, which is largely paid by residents and by public programs like Medicaid [S3].

The bill does not ban arbitration outright—residents could still choose to arbitrate after a dispute arises—but by invalidating all pre-dispute agreements it removes even voluntarily bargained-for arbitration terms, which some would see as overbroad [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to residents is concrete and one-sided in the common case: a family facing neglect or wrongful death keeps the option of a public court proceeding instead of a confidential arbitration chosen by the facility at admission. The cost falls on facility operators through higher litigation exposure, and some of that cost may pass through to residents and public payers. On balance the bill's design—banning pre-dispute clauses while leaving post-dispute arbitration available—targets the practice most criticized, signing away rights before any dispute exists, without eliminating arbitration entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez introduced the bill on August 2, 2012, joined by three Democratic cosponsors—Reps. Conyers, Carson, and Schakowsky—and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1, S3, S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S5].
With the 112th Congress ending on January 3, 2013, a bill that never left committee expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Long-term care facilities keep the ability to require residents to sign arbitration agreements at admission, keeping neglect and abuse claims in confidential arbitration rather than public court. Residents and families gained nothing from this outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators who use arbitration clauses

for.name: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee on August 2, 2012.

for.name: Reps. John Conyers, André Carson, and Jan Schakowsky

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; never scheduled action
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing or markup—so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Long-term care industry
against.role: Operators of nursing homes and assisted-living facilities
against.what_they_did: Opposed similar arbitration restrictions in Congress and at federal agencies on the ground that arbitration controls liability costs; the bill's referral to a committee that did not act ended it without floor debate.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and the bill received no Republican cosponsors; it also received no floor vote, so there was no recorded partisan split beyond the sponsorship pattern.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care operators
industries.note: The bill would strip operators of pre-dispute arbitration agreements, which keep neglect, abuse, and wrongful-death claims out of public court where damages tend to be larger and records public. The industry's interest in keeping those clauses runs against residents' access to court.

Mandatory pre-dispute arbitration in nursing home admissions is a steady source of cases for private arbitration providers; the bill would cut off that stream at the source, though post-dispute arbitration would remain available.
